source_title: Small and Medium Enterprises in the Pandemic: Impact, Responses and the Role of Development Finance (World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 9414)
publisher_issuer: World Bank Group (Policy Research Working Paper 9414), based on World Bank Enterprise Survey / Business Pulse Survey data
company_context: A cross-country World Bank study of how micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in developing economies fared during the COVID-19 pandemic, drawing on World Bank Enterprise Survey follow-ups and Business Pulse Surveys. It quantifies the small-business liquidity and cash-flow squeeze relative to larger firms.
business_type: Aggregate small and medium enterprises (cross-sector, developing economies)
macro_context: COVID-19 demand and supply shocks, lockdowns and mobility restrictions that disproportionately hit smaller firms with thinner cash buffers and weaker access to credit.
outcome_category: 7 - severe liquidity / cash-flow crisis (population-level small business)
evidence_summary: The paper finds that SMEs were under intense strain during the pandemic, with more than half of firms either in arrears or likely to fall into arrears shortly. SMEs were more likely than larger firms to report decreased liquidity or cash-flow availability, by an average of about 10 percentage points. On average, SMEs were estimated to have liquidity to cover fixed costs for only about 10 weeks, roughly 3 weeks less than larger firms. Approximately one-third of firms experienced a temporary closure at some point, rising to about 37% of firms during the survey's second wave. Medium-sized firms were the most vulnerable to temporary closures.

source_backed_metrics.sme_avg_weeks_liquidity_for_fixed_costs: approximately 10 weeks (about 3 weeks less than larger firms)
source_backed_metrics.share_firms_temporary_closure: approximately one-third (rising to ~37% in the second survey wave)

owner_decision_context: Small-business owners faced acute cash-runway decisions under the shock: whether to defer payments (risking arrears), cut costs/lay off staff, draw on scarce credit, or temporarily close, with materially less liquidity buffer than larger competitors.
action_taken: At the population level, responses documented include temporary closures, workforce reductions, falling into arrears, and dependence on development-finance and government support facilities to bridge cash-flow gaps.
outcome_evidence: Quantified findings (majority in/near arrears, ~10pp larger liquidity decline than big firms, ~10 weeks of fixed-cost coverage, ~one-third experiencing temporary closures) confirm a pervasive small-business cash/liquidity crisis driven by an exogenous demand shock rather than firm-specific mismanagement.
source_limitations: WebFetch of the World Bank PDF returned HTTP 403; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets that quote this exact working paper (PRWP 9414) and the related Enterprise Survey follow-up report. These are population-level statistics, not a single named company, so they support a small-business archetype rather than one firm's trajectory.
directly_stated: More than half of firms in arrears or likely to fall into arrears shortly
SMEs reported decreased liquidity/cash flow ~10 percentage points more than larger firms
SMEs had on average ~10 weeks of liquidity for fixed costs, ~3 weeks less than larger firms
About one-third of firms experienced temporary closure, rising to ~37% in the second wave
inferred: Thin cash buffers, not insolvency per se, were the binding constraint for most small firms in the shock
Smaller firms' disadvantage was structural (less credit access, lower reserves) rather than performance-driven
why_useful_for_opsiq: Provides a credible, government/institutional small-business benchmark for a cash-liquidity crisis driven by an external shock, balancing the pool's large-cap and US skew. Tests whether the engine correctly classifies an exogenous-shock liquidity crisis (short runway, arrears) for a small firm and distinguishes it from unit-economics or governance failure.
